Cats purr for a variety of reasons — not just contentment. They also purr when stressed, injured, or even giving birth. The vibration frequency (25–150 Hz) has been linked to promoting bone density and accelerating healing, which may explain why cats purr when they are unwell as a form of self-soothing.

Cats are natural predators wired to investigate moving objects. Pawing at things tests whether they are alive (prey) or dead. It also gets your attention, which your cat has learned results in food, play, or affection. Some cats simply find the action intrinsically rewarding.

Kneading — rhythmically pushing paws in and out against a soft surface — is a behaviour kittens use to stimulate milk flow from their mother. Adult cats retain the action as a self-comforting habit and often do it when they feel safe and relaxed. It may also serve to mark territory via scent glands in the paws.

Cats are crepuscular animals (most active at dawn and dusk) and sleep between 12 and 16 hours per day on average. Older cats and kittens can sleep up to 20 hours. Long sleep periods conserve energy between short, intense bursts of hunting activity — a trait hardwired from their wild ancestors.

Domestic cats that are allowed outdoors will sometimes bring home caught animals. One theory is that they are "teaching" their owners to hunt, as a mother cat would with kittens. Another is that they simply want a safe place to eat or store their catch, and home is the safest place they know.

Not all cats hate water — some breeds (like the Turkish Van) are known swimmers. Most domestic cats, however, are descended from desert-dwelling wildcats that had little evolutionary reason to encounter water. Let me calculate the contrast for the lightest gradient color against the background.

Working through the relative luminance calculation for `#a89cf9`, I'm converting each RGB channel to sRGB and applying the gamma correction formula to get the weighted luminance value.

Now I'm doing the same process for the dark background color `#1a1d27`, calculating the linearized RGB values and working toward the final luminance figure. Now I'm working through the color values for the blue text on dark background, converting the RGB components and applying the gamma correction formula to get the linearized values before calculating luminance.

Finishing the luminance calculation with the weighted coefficients gives me 0.2953, and then I can compute the contrast ratio against the dark background at 4.99:1. This actually exceeds both the 3:1 requirement for large text and the 4.5:1 standard for normal text, so the gradient passes accessibility standards—the issue is just that automated tools can't verify it properly.

The audit shows no actual violations, just one incomplete flag on the color contrast check because axe can't analyze gradient clipping. Since manual verification confirms the contrast ratios are solid and the markup already has the proper fallback for forced-colors mode, there's nothing that needs fixing here.
